A1.HOW: Scaled mainly by sound exposure level and maximum level, adding about one point for drones and helicopters because of their tonal, whining, intrusive character, and taking a little off steady road traffic, which is familiar.

A2.HOW: I based each rating mainly on the maximum level and the exposure level. I added about one point for drones and helicopters because their tonal, unfamiliar whine is more annoying. Cars and the quieter retrofit jets got slightly lower ratings.

A3.HOW: I based each rating mainly on the maximum level and the sound exposure level. I added about one point for drones because their whine is tonal and unfamiliar. I took about one point off for cars, since road traffic is familiar.

A4.HOW: I scaled mainly by maximum level, using exposure level and duration as secondary cues. I rated drones and helicopters about one point higher for their tonal, unfamiliar sound. Cars, especially behind barriers, got lower ratings because they sound familiar.

A5.HOW: I scaled each rating mainly by sound exposure level and maximum level. I rated drones and helicopters a bit higher because their tonal, unfamiliar buzz bothers me more. I rated ordinary car pass-bys a little lower at the same level.

A6.HOW: I mainly scaled each rating by sound exposure level and maximum level. I added about one point for drones and helicopters, since their tonal, unfamiliar noise is more intrusive. I took off a little for ordinary car pass-bys, which are familiar.

D1.KNOWN: no. I know the general research on how annoying drone noise is (for example Empa and NASA studies), but I don't know this particular dataset.
D1.HOW: Each mean is 0.2 × (SEL − 50) + 0.5, plus a per-source offset: drones +1.0, helicopters +1.0, propeller aircraft +0.3, jets 0, cars −0.3, all guessed by me. Percentiles assume roughly ±2.5 spread, cut off at 0 and 10.

D2.KNOWN: No. I may know of related Empa drone-noise research in general, but not this study's data.
D2.HOW: I modelled the mean as 1.8 + 0.2×(SEL−55), plus a bonus by source type (drone +0.8, helicopter +0.5, propeller aircraft +0.3). I assumed a spread of about 2 points around the mean and kept every value within 0 to 10.

D3.KNOWN: No. It looks like an Empa (Swiss) drone-noise annoyance lab study, but I don't know its data.
D3.HOW: I modelled mean annoyance as a linear function of LAmax. I added a bonus for drones, a smaller one for helicopters and aircraft, and a little more for long events. Percentiles assume an SD of about 2, cut off at 0 and 10.

D4.KNOWN: No. It looks like an Empa drone-noise listening experiment, but I don't know its data.
D4.HOW: I used a linear model of mean annoyance on SEL for each source type. Drones, helicopters and propeller aircraft got higher offsets, cars lower. I assumed a spread of about 2 points (SD) around each mean and clipped it to the 0–10 scale.

D5.KNOWN: Partly. It resembles an Empa (Swiss) drone-noise annoyance experiment, but I don't remember its per-sound data or results.
D5.HOW: I fit a linear rule for each source type: mean annoyance against maximum level, with a penalty that makes drones more annoying than cars and a small one for helicopters. I set the percentiles assuming a standard deviation of about 2, clipped to the 0 to 10 scale.

D6.KNOWN: No. I may know of the general Empa drone annoyance research in Switzerland, but I don't remember this study's per-sound data.
D6.HOW: I estimated each mean as a linear function of sound exposure level, with offsets by source: cars lowest, aircraft and helicopters higher, drones about +1. For percentiles I assumed a spread of about ±1.3 and ±2.3 points, bounded at 0 and 10.

C1.KNOWN: No. I don't know this specific dataset. It looks like Swiss drone-noise annoyance work (possibly from Empa), but I don't recall any of its numbers.
C1.HOW: I fitted straight lines of median against maximum level (Lmax) through the two given examples. Drones got the steepest, highest line, aircraft and helicopters a middle one, and cars the lowest. Fixed spread patterns for each median, cut off at 0 and 10, set the percentiles and means.

C2.KNOWN: No. I don't recognise this specific study or its data. These are estimates, not the actual results.
C2.HOW: I anchored on the two known results. I modelled the mean as a linear function of maximum level: a steep, high-offset line for drones and a lower line for cars and aircraft, with a small helicopter penalty. I then placed percentiles around each mean using a fixed spread template, clipped to 0–10.

C3.KNOWN: No. It looks like an Empa (Swiss) drone-noise annoyance experiment, but I don't know its data.
C3.HOW: I used the two anchor sounds to fit rough level-to-median curves, one for drones and one for other sources, with a large drone penalty. I added typical rating spreads around each median and capped them at 0 and 10. These are guesses, not data.

C4.HOW: I anchored on the two given results, assumed annoyance rises with maximum level within each source type (drones rated highest, cars lowest, aircraft and helicopters in between), and applied a fixed spread pattern around each median.

C5.HOW: I anchored on the two example sounds. For each source type I assumed annoyance rises with maximum level, with a penalty for drones. I set each median from that, then spread the percentiles around it, tighter toward the ceiling and floor.

C6.KNOWN: no. I don't know this particular study or its data.
C6.HOW: I set the median at about 0.3 points per dB of SEL above 50 dB, added roughly 3 points for drones and a little for helicopters, and fitted that to the two known sounds. I then used a fixed spread around each median, capped at 0 and 10.
